overview.what_it_is: This lesson reviews whole numbers, operations, factors, and fractions. It joins many earlier skills in one practice set.

format_facts.label: Main sections
format_facts.value: Place value, operations, factors, fractions, and word problems

format_facts.label: Answer style
format_facts.value: Show each step, then write a clear answer sentence

format_facts.label: Checking
format_facts.value: Use estimation, inverse operations, and sensible units

scoring_factors.name: Correct answer
scoring_factors.what_it_measures: Whether the final number is right.

scoring_factors.name: Clear working
scoring_factors.what_it_measures: Whether each maths step can be followed.

scoring_factors.name: Method choice
scoring_factors.what_it_measures: Whether the chosen method fits the question.

scoring_factors.name: Units
scoring_factors.what_it_measures: Whether money, length, mass, or time is named.

scoring_factors.name: Reasonable check
scoring_factors.what_it_measures: Whether the answer makes sense for the question.

critical_rules: Read every place value from right to left.
For rounding, check the digit just to the right.
Estimate before long multiplication or long division.
Do brackets before multiplication, division, addition, and subtraction.
Make fraction bottom numbers match before adding or subtracting.
Make each fraction as simple as possible.
For whole-number division, always state any remainder.
Use a bar model before solving a word problem.

learning_goals: You will read large numbers in figures and words.
You will find a digit's value in a large number.
You will round numbers to the nearest thousand.
You will estimate sums, differences, products, and quotients.
You will find factors and multiples shared by two numbers.
You will use the correct order of operations.
You will change mixed numbers and improper fractions.
You will compare, order, add, subtract, multiply, and divide fractions.
You will solve one-step and multi-step word problems.

core_method.name: Read → Picture → Choose → Work → Answer → Check
core_method.summary: First read the task. Choose one fitting method. Show the steps. Then check the answer.

steps.detail: Circle the numbers, units, and task words.
Use a place chart, number line, or bar model.
Pick the rule that matches the question.
Write one clear maths step at a time.
State the result with the correct unit.
Estimate or use the opposite operation.

techniques.name: Build a place-value chart
techniques.purpose: Shows what each digit is worth.
how_to: Start with the ones place on the right.
Move left through tens, hundreds, and thousands.
Put each digit in one place only.
Read each three-digit group from left to right.
techniques.why_it_matters: A digit changes value when its place changes.
techniques.common_error: Reading the digit itself, not its place value.

techniques.name: Round with the next digit
how_to: Find the place named in the question.
Look at the digit just to its right.
Keep the digit if the next digit is small.
Raise it by one if the next digit is five or more.
techniques.why_it_matters: Rounding helps you estimate and check answers.
techniques.common_error: Looking at the wrong digit when deciding.

techniques.name: Use friendly numbers
techniques.purpose: Makes an estimate easy to work out.
how_to: Round each number to a useful place.
Choose numbers that work well together.
Do the easier operation.
Write the estimate sign, not an equals sign.
techniques.why_it_matters: The estimate tells you the answer's likely size.
techniques.common_error: Treating an estimate as the exact answer.

techniques.name: List factors and multiples
techniques.purpose: Finds numbers shared by two number sets.
how_to: List factor pairs for each number.
Circle the factors found in both lists.
For multiples, count up in each number.
Stop at the first or any shared multiple.
techniques.example: $8$ is a common factor of $24$ and $32$. Also, $40$ is a common multiple of $8$ and $10$.
techniques.why_it_matters: Shared factors help make fractions simpler.

techniques.name: Follow operation order
techniques.purpose: Keeps mixed calculations in the right order.
how_to: Work inside brackets first.
Do multiplication and division from left to right.
Do addition and subtraction from left to right.
Check by reading the expression again.
techniques.why_it_matters: Changing the order can change the answer.
techniques.common_error: Always working from left to right.

techniques.name: Change fraction forms
techniques.purpose: Moves between mixed numbers and top-heavy fractions.
how_to: For a mixed number, multiply whole by bottom.
Add the top number.
Keep the same bottom number.
For the reverse, divide top by bottom.
techniques.why_it_matters: Some fraction operations are easier in one form.
techniques.common_error: Adding the whole number straight to the top.

techniques.name: Make shared bottoms
techniques.purpose: Lets you compare, add, or subtract fractions.
how_to: Find a bottom number both fractions can use.
Change each fraction without changing its value.
Work with the top numbers.
Make the final fraction simpler.
techniques.why_it_matters: Equal-sized parts are needed before combining them.

techniques.name: Draw a bar model
techniques.purpose: Shows parts, wholes, and what is unknown.
how_to: Draw one bar for the whole amount.
Split it into the parts named.
Label known parts and the unknown part.
Choose operations from the picture.
techniques.example: For $600$ cookies in groups of $24$, draw equal groups. Then use $600 \div 24 = 25$.
techniques.why_it_matters: The picture stops you choosing the wrong operation.
techniques.common_error: Using every number before knowing its job.

worked_examples.title: Round a large number
worked_examples.decoding: The answer must be a whole number of thousands.
worked_examples.plan: Find the thousands digit. Then check the hundreds digit.
worked_examples.model_answer: The thousands digit is $7$. The hundreds digit is $5$. A $5$ means round up. So $437{,}549 \approx 438{,}000$. The rounded number is $438{,}000$.

annotations.comment: This digit is in the thousands place.
This digit decides whether we round up.
This sign means the value is close.
All places after thousands become zero.

worked_examples.title: Estimate a product
worked_examples.decoding: The word estimate asks for a nearby answer.
worked_examples.plan: Round both numbers to friendly values, then multiply.

annotations.comment: This is close to $4{,}825$.
This is close to $63$.
This gives the likely size of the answer.
Use this sign because the answer is estimated.

worked_examples.title: Correct the operation order
worked_examples.decoding: Brackets and division must happen before the final sums.
worked_examples.plan: Do brackets. Do division. Then work left to right.
worked_examples.model_answer: First, $(6 + 25) = 31$. Next, $21 \div 3 = 7$. Now work left to right: $78 + 7 - 31 = 85 - 31 = 54$. The value of the expression is $54$.

annotations.comment: Brackets are completed first.
Division comes before addition and subtraction.
The last two operations go left to right.
A quick estimate confirms this is sensible.

worked_examples.title: Divide with a remainder
worked_examples.decoding: The groups may not divide exactly.
worked_examples.plan: Find the largest multiple of $24$ below $301$.
worked_examples.model_answer: We know $24 \times 12 = 288$. Subtract to find what remains: $301 - 288 = 13$. So $301 \div 24 = 12 \text{ r } 13$. As a mixed number, this is $12\frac{13}{24}$. The quotient is $12$ with remainder $13$.

annotations.comment: This is the largest fitting multiple.
This finds the amount left over.
The remainder is stated clearly.
The remainder can also form a fraction.

worked_examples.title: Change to a mixed number
worked_examples.input: Write $\frac{20}{6}$ as a mixed number in simplest form.
worked_examples.decoding: Divide the top number by the bottom number.
worked_examples.plan: Find the whole groups, write the remainder, then reduce.
worked_examples.model_answer: Divide: $20 \div 6 = 3 \text{ r } 2$. So $\frac{20}{6} = 3\frac{2}{6}$. The fraction part can be reduced: $\frac{2}{6} = \frac{1}{3}$. Therefore, $\frac{20}{6} = 3\frac{1}{3}$. The mixed number is $3\frac{1}{3}$.

annotations.comment: There are three complete groups of six.
Two parts remain after the division.
The remainder goes over the old bottom.
Both numbers were divided by two.

worked_examples.title: Add fractions with different bottoms
worked_examples.decoding: The bottom numbers differ, so make them match.
worked_examples.plan: Use twelfths, add the tops, then change the form.
worked_examples.model_answer: The smallest shared bottom is $12$. Change both fractions: $\frac{5}{6} = \frac{10}{12}$ and $\frac{3}{4} = \frac{9}{12}$. Add: $\frac{10}{12} + \frac{9}{12} = \frac{19}{12}$. Change the form: $19 \div 12 = 1 \text{ r } 7$. So $\frac{19}{12} = 1\frac{7}{12}$. The sum is $1\frac{7}{12}$.

annotations.comment: Both sixths and quarters can become twelfths.
The top and bottom were both doubled.
The top and bottom were both tripled.
The answer is written as a mixed number.

worked_examples.title: Order four fractions
worked_examples.decoding: Change each value into an easy form for comparison.
worked_examples.plan: Compare whole parts first. Then compare fraction parts.
worked_examples.model_answer: Change the top-heavy fractions: $\frac{9}{4} = 2\frac{1}{4}$ and $\frac{9}{2} = 4\frac{1}{2}$. Compare the two numbers near $1$: $1\frac{3}{4} = 1\frac{6}{8}$. Since $1\frac{5}{8} < 1\frac{6}{8}$, it comes first. Therefore, $1\frac{5}{8} < 1\frac{3}{4} < \frac{9}{4} < \frac{9}{2}$. This is the order from smallest to greatest.

annotations.comment: This shows $\frac{9}{4}$ is more than two.
This is clearly the largest value.
Eighths make the close pair easy to compare.
This sign means the left value is smaller.

worked_examples.title: Solve an equal-group word problem
worked_examples.input: Ashley packs $600$ cookies into packets of $24$. How many packets are made?
worked_examples.decoding: The total and each group size are known.
worked_examples.plan: Bar model: one bar shows $600$ cookies. Split it into equal parts of $24$ cookies.
worked_examples.model_answer: The number of packets is $600 \div 24$. Since $24 \times 25 = 600$, we get $600 \div 24 = 25$. Ashley makes $25$ packets.

annotations.comment: The bar stands for all $600$ cookies.
Each packet contains the same number.
Division finds how many equal groups fit.
The answer includes the correct item name.

worked_examples.title: Solve a multi-step fraction problem
worked_examples.input: David had $1{,}280$ eggs. He sold $\frac{3}{5}$ on Saturday. He sold $\frac{1}{4}$ of the remainder on Sunday. How many eggs did he sell altogether?
worked_examples.decoding: Sunday's fraction is taken from the new remainder.
worked_examples.plan: Bar model: split the whole into fifths. Remove three fifths. Then split the remaining part into quarters.
worked_examples.model_answer: Saturday sales were $\frac{3}{5} \times 1{,}280 = 3 \times 256 = 768$ eggs. The remainder was $1{,}280 - 768 = 512$ eggs. Sunday sales were $\frac{1}{4} \times 512 = 128$ eggs. Total sales were $768 + 128 = 896$ eggs. David sold $896$ eggs altogether.

annotations.comment: This finds Saturday's sales.
Sunday's fraction uses this remainder.
This finds Sunday's sales.
Both days are added for the total.

items.when_to_use: Name one symbol from zero to nine.
Say what a digit is worth in its place.
Replace a number with a nearby easy number.
Give a close answer before exact working.
Name the answer from addition.
Name the answer from subtraction.
Name the answer from multiplication.
Name the main answer from division.
Name what is left after equal grouping.
Say a number divides with nothing left.
Describe sets with the same amount.
Multiply after division to check the result.
Count how many parts are being used.
Name the bottom number once, then say bottom.
Write a whole number with a fraction.
Write a fraction with top larger than bottom.
Look for a total, often found by adding.
Find the difference between two amounts.
Multiply when finding a fraction of an amount.
Subtract used, sold, or removed parts.

common_mistakes.mistake: Reading a digit without using its place.
common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: The value can be thousands or millions larger.
common_mistakes.fix: Name the place first, then write the value.

common_mistakes.mistake: Rounding from the wrong nearby digit.
common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: The rounded number moves in the wrong direction.
common_mistakes.fix: Look only one place to the right.

common_mistakes.mistake: Writing an equals sign for an estimate.
common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: An estimate is close, but not always exact.
The two number lists follow different rules.
common_mistakes.fix: Factors divide in. Multiples count up.

common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: The operation order changes the result.
common_mistakes.fix: Do brackets, multiplication, and division first.

common_mistakes.mistake: Hiding a remainder in whole-number division.

common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: The parts no longer have the right size.
common_mistakes.fix: Make bottoms match, then add only the tops.

common_mistakes.mistake: Leaving a fraction in a larger form.
common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: The value is right but not fully finished.
common_mistakes.fix: Divide top and bottom by a shared factor.

common_mistakes.mistake: Using the original whole after some was removed.
common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: A later fraction may use the remainder instead.
common_mistakes.fix: Draw a new bar for the amount left.

common_mistakes.mistake: Forgetting units in the final sentence.
common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: The reader cannot tell what the number means.
common_mistakes.fix: Write dollars, metres, eggs, packets, or another unit.

time_budget.focus: Times tables and easy fraction facts
Exact work, remainders, and operation order
Correct errors and explain two answers

drills.name: Place-value sprint
drills.instructions: Write four large numbers in words. Then name one digit's value.

drills.name: Rounding ladder
drills.instructions: Round six numbers to the nearest $1{,}000$.

drills.name: Estimate first
drills.instructions: Estimate four operations before finding exact answers.

drills.name: Factor and multiple pairs
drills.instructions: Find one common factor and multiple for four pairs.

drills.name: Order challenge
drills.instructions: Solve six mixed expressions using the correct order.

drills.name: Fraction form swap
drills.instructions: Change four mixed numbers and four improper fractions.

drills.name: Fraction operation set
drills.instructions: Do two adds, two subtracts, two products, and two divisions.

drills.name: Bar-model stories
drills.instructions: Draw bars for three word problems before using numbers.

practice_plan.routine: Work in short sets. Check each set at once. Redo every wrong item without looking.

mastery_checklist: I can write large numbers in figures and words.
I can state the value of any digit.
I can round to the nearest thousand.
I can choose friendly numbers for an estimate.
I can find a shared factor or multiple.
I can multiply and divide large whole numbers.
I can state a division remainder clearly.
I can follow the correct operation order.
I can change between both fraction forms.
I can compare and order fractions.
I can work with fractions in all four operations.
I can use a bar model for word problems.
strategy_notes: Underline what the question asks before working.
Estimate first when the exact numbers are large.
Write one maths step on each new line.
Check division by multiplying the quotient back.
Check fraction answers are in the simplest form.
Compare whole parts before comparing fraction parts.
Keep units beside numbers during word problems.
When a problem says remainder, use the new amount.
Do not copy a listed answer without checking it.
Save five minutes to review signs, units, and remainders.
